raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1,2]. Historically viewed as an ultra-rare, untreatable condition, CA is increasingly recognized as a major underdiagnosed cause of heart failure (HF), particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [3,4]. The two primary amyloid proteins that infiltrate the myocardium are monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL amyloidosis) and transthyretin (ATTR amyloidosis) [5-7]. AL amyloidosis is a hematologic disorder stemming from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia [8,9]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis results from the dissociation of the hepatic-derived transthyretin homotetramer and can manifest as either hereditary (ATTRv, "v" for variant) due to pathogenic mutations, or wild-type (ATTRwt) associated with aging [5,10,11].

### Clinical Presentation and Red Flags
The clinical presentation of CA is characterized by systemic and cardiac symptoms. Refractory HF, conduction system disease, and atrial fibrillation are frequent cardiac manifestations of CA [1,7,12]. Extracardiac "red flags" are crucial for early clinical recognition; these include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic neuropathy [6,13]. Notably, ATTRwt is highly prevalent among older men presenting with HFpEF, aortic stenosis, and carpal tunnel syndrome [4,10]. In contrast, AL amyloidosis represents a medical emergency, presenting with rapid-onset heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, macroglossia, and cutaneous purpura [8,14].

### Diagnostic Advances: The Shift to Non-Invasive Algorithms
Diagnosing CA has undergone a paradigm shift over the last decade. Classically, definitive diagnosis required an endomyocardial biopsy showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo red staining [1,2]. However, non-invasive diagnostic algorithms have revolutionized clinical practice [6,15]. 

An initial screening workup involves assessing for a monoclonal protein using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chain (sFLC) assays [6,16]. Concurrently, technetium-99m-pyrophosphate ($^{99m}\text{Tc-PYP}$) or bone-seeking tracer scintigraphy (such as DPD or HMDP) is performed [15,17]. In the absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, a Grade 2 or 3 cardiac uptake on bone scintigraphy has a specificity and positive predictive value of nearly 100% for ATTR cardiomyopathy, which safely obviates the need for endomyocardial biopsy [15,17].

Multimodality imaging plays a fundamental role in evaluating suspected patients [18]. Electrocardiography (ECG) often displays low voltage relative to the degree of ventricular wall thickness, though this classic mismatch is not universally present [7]. Echocardiography typically reveals concentric ventricular hypertrophy, biatrial enlargement, and a classic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [5,19]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides exquisite tissue characterization; diffuse late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), elevated native T1 times, and increased extracellular volume (ECV) are highly sensitive and specific diagnostic and prognostic markers [20,21].

### Management and Therapeutic Breakthroughs
The therapeutic landscape of CA has dramatically evolved from supportive care to targeted disease-modifying therapies. In AL amyloidosis, rapid hematologic response is paramount to limit ongoing cardiotoxicity [22,23]. The current standard of care for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis includes the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone, which has demonstrated superior hematologic and organ response rates [9,24]. Supportive chemotherapy combinations have historically included melphalan and dexamethasone, followed by autologous stem cell transplantation in eligible patients [25,26].

For ATTR amyloidosis, the landmark ATTR-ACT trial established tafamidis—a small-molecule TTR stabilizer that prevents tetramer dissociation—as the first-line therapy [27]. Tafamidis significantly reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in patients with ATTRwt and ATTRv cardiomyopathy [27]. Additionally, genetic silencing therapies that inhibit hepatic production of TTR have emerged. The RNA interference (RNAi) therapeutics patisiran and vutrisiran, along with the antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) inotersen, have demonstrated efficacy in halting or reversing neuropathy in ATTRv [28,29]. More recently, patisiran has demonstrated beneficial effects on functional capacity and cardiac parameters in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [30].

### Conclusion and Future Directions
Recent multidisciplinary guidelines highlight the necessity of early detection and specialized collaborative care for patients with CA [6,19]. With the advent of highly effective therapies and streamlined non-invasive diagnostic pathways, early screening in at-risk populations remains the most critical step to prevent irreversible myocardial damage and improve long-term survival.
